question: How should mayors prepare for scaled up testing if and when these it’s possible?
original answer:
Every test has a particular false-negative rate, and sometimes a false-positive rate, and results may differ when tests are taken on different days. When people are just getting sick, false negatives are not uncommon. If someone has symptoms and test results are inconclusive, physicians should treat the person like they're positive. Sometimes, when there's enough of a story—e.g., someone says, "I've lost my sense of smell. I'm coughing”—even if the test is negative, you treat it like a case.

Tests have strengths and weaknesses. Short answer: when results conflict, assume the patient has coronavirus. (Dr. Josh Sharfstein, 5/19/20)

Contact tracing is the tool to get us out of this crisis safely. We should be putting as much energy as possible into scaling those capabilities. Communities are saying this is new for them; they're not sure how this works, but contact tracing is something we do all the time in public health—for sexually transmitted infections, pertussis, and measles. It's really about scaling those capabilities, supporting people as they undergo isolation and quarantine and helping to keep our communities safe. The more you can talk to your communities about that, the smoother it will go. (Dr. Caitlin Rivers, 5/26/20)

question: How effective are masks for slowing transmission?
original answer:
Health care workers’ masks are very effective. But there aren't enough for all of us to be able to wear them. Instead, CDC recommends fabric face masks. They are required for us here in Maryland, and I wear one every time I go outside. They are fairly good at protecting other people. This virus is spread largely through droplets that we emit when we talk, cough, and so on, and the masks help to contain the droplets.

We don't think the masks are very effective at protecting the wearer from infection, however. There’s a powerful phrase: "My mask protects you, and your mask protects me." If we all wear them, it is a powerful intervention. But the individual-level protection is less pronounced. (Dr. Caitlin Rivers, 5/26/20)

A real concern is that people wearing masks won’t feel they need to socially distance. They do. The general idea masks are better than none makes sense, but efficacy depends on the mask, how it's used, and the risk of harm if not used properly. Nothing is perfect here. The key is not to suggest these tools are going to fully protect people. (Dr. Jennifer Nuzzo, 5/13/20)

Also, requiring masks shouldn't be used as an excuse not to set up other protective barriers like plexiglass to protect essential workers. (Dr. Josh Sharfstein, 5/13/20)

question: How should we address the potential civil liberties or legal risks to requiring mask or temperature checks?
original answer:
Mask requirements generally are issued through local ordinances and regulations, not criminal law. A penalty will likely be either a talking-to or a fine with no privacy implications, no different from a seatbelt law or something like that.

What mayors need to look out for is racial bias in enforcement. In New York City, police were antagonizing African American citizens who were not wearing masks in one neighborhood, while other officers were handing out masks to predominantly white New Yorkers in Central Park. You want to make sure you treat different communities the same, and enforcement should never be hostile.

Remember the difference between rights and privileges. No one has a right to enter, say, a courtroom or federal facility, without a security check. We're just going to have to view temperature checks as the equivalent of security checks—as an essential part of public safety and security.

There may be legal challenges from individuals who want access to a private club or bar that insists they undergo a temperature check, but I think these would fall apart because no one has a right to go to a bar. I think we are on very solid footing with these orders. Some of you know that the Wisconsin Supreme Court overruled the governor yesterday. But as it hits the federal courts, there will be new case law on this, and I think it's going to be pro-community. (Juliette Kayyem, 5/20/20)

question: How have cities celebrated high school graduates who are missing important events such as graduation and prom?
original answer:
While many school districts have postponed graduation or prom, others are planning alternatives to give high school seniors a proper send off. For example, New York City will host a city-wide virtual graduation ceremony for all high school seniors. Other cities and towns are holding ceremonies in drive-in movie theaters, parking lots, or racetracks. In South Bend, the Parent Teacher Association surprised graduating high school seniors by hand-delivering lawn signs to their homes. At Homewood-Flossmoor High School in Chicago, the school’s broadcasting and film teachers are using the school’s student-run television and radio stations to plan a virtual prom.

Other school districts have looked outside their school systems to offer students a graduation or prom experience. MTV has partnered with Michelle Obama’s voter registration organization to host a virtual “Prom-athon” on MTV’s YouTube channel on May 22. Many social media platforms are hosting special online graduation events for seniors with celebrity guest speakers. Vulture Media has published a comprehensive list of virtual graduation ceremonies here.

question: How accurate are antibody tests?
original answer:
On April 28th, the FDA issued emergency use authorization for antibody tests. There are over 120 antibody tests available, but only 12 had been authorized by the FDA as of May 15. It is not yet clear that the presence of antibodies suggests immunity to the virus. (Dr. Josh Sharfstein, 5/19/20)

Antibody tests aim to measure the body’s response to a coronavirus infection. These turn positive about five days after the onset of symptoms and can stay positive for weeks or months. There are many antibody tests on the market, but some of these are of low quality. Over the next few weeks, we hope to see a sorting out of which antibody tests are the most accurate.

Some people are saying that having antibodies is the same as being immune to coronavirus infection. Whether this is actually true, however, is not yet known. There is ongoing research to determine the extent to which antibody levels means that someone is not likely to become sick with coronavirus again. As a result, it is too soon to consider using antibody tests for “immune certificates” or other ideas that have been proposed. (Dr. Josh Sharfstein, 4/21/20)

question: When you need authorization to try something from other levels of government that may be slow to respond or risk averse, how do those of us on the frontlines convey the urgency and speed things up?
original answer:
One option is to say that—based on sound public health guidance—you are going to advance on a certain day unless you hear otherwise. In other words, you don't need approval, you're just asking for it. That's going to focus them on your request rather than the 100 others they are juggling.

A second option is to remind them that there's really no right answer at this stage but there is one wrong answer, which is being too late.

You can also propose a pilot. In other words, ask that they let you try something for a week or two, assess how it's going, and then bring it down or ratchet up, depending on results. You give them more options than an on-off switch, and sometimes that brings clarity. (Juliette Kayyem, 5/20/20)

If there's one level of government that seems afraid to try something different, you may want to ask around or even come to us. Local officials who have wanted to do extra testing and been told “no” have come to us, and we've put the question to the state and the answer comes back “yes.” It's not necessarily the case that everyone along the chain is opposed to your idea. Sometimes you can keep raising the question until you find somebody who's going to say, actually that would help me. Then you can find a face-saving way to proceed. (Dr. Josh Sharfstein, 5/19/20)

question: How should we navigate the many uncertainties associated with innovating?
original answer:
One of the most important things you can do is reframe and recharacterize this discussion from a political discussion to a community innovation discussion. Keep bringing the focus of your team, and your other constituents, back to the goal – of building the future together – always setting a positive example of the messages and behaviors that you want others to embody as well. 

The current requirement to wear masks in public provides a small example of a leadership opportunity, meaning that with the right leadership—yours—you have an opportunity to emphasize the value of caring about others and to model the behavior that demonstrates that caring.  By modeling a behavior, with the visibility of your position, you make it something that people want to do. Your job is to inspire and tap into intrinsic motivation. The fear of punishment is not as effective as inspiring people’s desire to live up to the community’s values.

Mayors also have a real opportunity to help the public avoid the false dichotomy of caring about the economy versus caring about health. The opportunity is to switch from an “either/or” frame to a “both/and” frame; what we need is new thinking on “how” – how best to enable economic activity without harming people. The practical question for every city is this: How do we navigate the new reality to help people remain healthy while gradually, carefully, and deliberately bringing back aspects of community life? It’s going to be iterative and involve experimentation. It is important to realize that this is a puzzle to be solved, not a decision to be made.  And by solving that puzzle carefully and thoughtfully, making many small changes along the way as you learn more, you will arrive at a good place. This is not something that Mayors can do alone. Solving this puzzle is decidedly a team sport. (Amy Edmondson, 5/19/20)

question: What do we do when multiple tests offer conflicting results?
original answer:
Every test has a particular false-negative rate, and sometimes a false-positive rate, and results may differ when tests are taken on different days. When people are just getting sick, false negatives are not uncommon. If someone has symptoms and test results are inconclusive, physicians should treat the person like they're positive. Sometimes, when there's enough of a story—e.g., someone says, "I've lost my sense of smell. I'm coughing”—even if the test is negative, you treat it like a case.

Tests have strengths and weaknesses. Short answer: when results conflict, assume the patient has coronavirus. (Dr. Josh Sharfstein, 5/19/20)

question: Are there ways to measure the economic impact of reopening to compare it to the immediate health risks?
original answer:
The economic toll inflicted by COVID-19 and the corresponding efforts to contain its spread has been devastating. Both workers and businesses as well as government’s fiscal capacity have been significantly affected by the crisis. Thus, as some jurisdictions have made progress in controlling the outbreak, demand for reopening businesses and increasing commercial opportunities has increased significantly. But too fast or widespread a reopening runs the risk of triggering further outbreaks and reversing any progress that has been made, not only in terms of protecting human health and but also with reinvigorating the economy. 

Closing was, ironically, the easy part.  As a city leader, you are now balancing three criteria to assess opening up: contact intensity (gyms are different than dry cleaners); number of contacts (500 is different than 5 people in an enclosed space); and the possibility of modifications to minimize the risks (PPE, one-way lanes in markets, limited seating, etc.)

It should also be noted that different jurisdictions will face considerably different sets of circumstances when assessing the risks. For instance, the economic impacts of COVID-19 are shaping up (so far) to be unevenly distributed across the United States.   Opportunity Insights Economic Tracker has information on the economic impacts of COVID-19 on people, businesses, and communities across the United States in real time. (Juliette Kayyem, 5/19/20)

question: As a city with a large hospitality industry how can we adapt with our largest revenue generators shuttered?
original answer:
Unfortunately, the hospitality industry will likely be one of the hardest hit industries as a result of the pandemic. Cities can take the following steps to support local hospitality companies during this difficult time:

·       Set up small business relief funds: Many cities are setting up small business relief funds to provide additional support to small businesses. These funds can be nimbler and more responsive to local concerns than funds dispersed through the SBA.

·       Find creative ways to partner with hospitality companies: Many hotels can be repurposed to house first responders, those in isolation or quarantine, or the elderly and other vulnerable populations. Partnering with these hotels can, in turn, help support them financially during this difficult time.

·       Encourage leniency on liabilities: Cities can allow business to defer or delay payments on any city taxes or fees (or encourage local lenders to extend repayment schedules) that allow businesses to retain their cash on hand for payroll.

·       Show support to businesses and workers: Cities can help bring attention to businesses that are still open, such as by highlighting different restaurants (including those in hotels / casinos / other hospitality companies) to their residents, noting the ways in which they have adapted, altered, or expanded their services.

·       Promote creativity with hospitality and event planners:  The event planning industry is also taking a huge hit but they are adapting by promoting different kinds of events, including having local residents stay at local hotels as a “conference get away.”  Connect with local and national event planning organizations and see how you might promote your city with their assistance.  (Juliette Kayyem, 5/19/20)

question: How should cities respond to restaurants opening in defiance of public health orders?
original answer:
One of the most important jobs of a mayor at this time is to continually stress the seriousness of the virus and the necessity of adhering to effective social distancing measures as long as the data indicates they are still needed to control the spread of the disease, preserve capacity within the healthcare system, and minimize deaths and serious illness within the community. Mayors can also communicate that they, too, want businesses to be able to re-open as soon as possible and should continually update local business owners about emerging plans to re-open. Such plans could feature phased re-openings, in which restaurants may first be allowed to focus on takeout and delivery, then offer outdoor and socially-distanced dining, and eventually some sort of indoor dining arrangement as conditions increasingly improve and certain benchmarks are met. In the end, though, defiance of a health order is either a civil or criminal violation and should be treated as such. 

Mayors also need not do this work alone. They can work through the local Chamber of Commerce or business advisory groups, who may have more sway with the restaurant(s) disregarding the policies. (In fact, making a concerted effort to engage with these stakeholders and treat them like partners may minimize such violations in and of itself – or lead to creative solutions city government may not consider on its own.) Using local health officials to help spread the message can help de-politicize the issue. Getting other employers from the same industry, such as other restaurant owners, to validate the orders publicly can also be useful.   And employing different tones can also be helpful. The City of Chicago, for example, has been using the recent viral popularity of a humorous meme to further encourage social distancing. These measures can prevent restaurants or other businesses from unlawfully re-opening in the first place. (Juliette Kayyem, 5/19/20)

question: How should I interpret data to understand whether we have achieved “robust” testing and effective contact tracing?
original answer:
Robust testing means that testing is available in sufficient quantities to cover priority groups. That's more important than an arbitrary number of tests being conducted. When we believe that we have enough capacity to reach the people who need to be tested, that it is well distributed and not just concentrated in one or two places, then we look at the positivity.

You want the overall percentage of positive test results to be low (<12%). If your rate of positive tests is high, above 2 percent, that suggests that you need to expand testing to fill in holes in the geographic coverage.

You want to look at new cases both by raw numbers and percentage from known contact lists. If the numbers of new cases are increasing, that's a bad sign, and means we have to do more testing. We would be slightly assuaged if we knew that cases were increasing, but those testing positive had already been under quarantine at home. That could suggest that we are capturing everybody while they're still incubating their infection and hopefully intervening before they can transmit it to others. When you find new cases, you want to see an increasing percentage of those cases coming from known contact lists. Ideally, it gets close to 100 percent, meaning that most new cases are people identified through robust contact tracing.  With contact tracing in place, we want to see that we are catching people before they become a known case and hopefully before they can transmit it to others. Eventually, you should see absolute cases going down as the percentage of cases from contact tracing lists goes up. (Dr. Jennifer Nuzzo, 5/13/20)

question: If new cases are coming almost exclusively or predominantly from nursing homes, how should we be factoring it into our decisions on reopening?
original answer:
It is important to break out that data because it can point to where interventions are needed. The challenge in protecting nursing homes is that the broader population-level restrictions are not very good at protecting them once the virus is in the facility. If you reduce the probability that the staff gets sick out in the community, there's less chance of bringing the virus in, but once you have cases in these facilities, the interventions are different.

It's hard to say, "Well, we're only having this increase in our nursing homes and therefore we're fine to reopen." You still have to protect nursing homes and also vulnerable individuals out in the population. If reopening leads to an increase in infections in the community, it will be harder to keep the virus out of nursing homes. (Dr. Jennifer Nuzzo, 5/13/20)

question: How should cities be monitoring the convergence of the upcoming seasonal flu season and ongoing COVID-19 crisis? What will be the metrics to watch for flu cases increasing, and when?
original answer:
Flu season severity, onset, and peak vary from year-to-year and are difficult to predict.  The CDC’s Influenza Division monitors influenza activity throughout the year and issues weekly surveillance reports during flu season. The CDC also updates an interactive online application, FluView Interactive, for more in-depth data. Cities can use these tools to monitor flu activity and severity. In recent years, the CDC started publishing these reports in late September or early October.

Additionally, U.S. health officials sometimes observe Australia’s flu season, which usually begins in June, as an potential indicator for severity of the upcoming U.S. flu season. Though, in some years, the flu season in the US and Australia differs in terms of severity, due to changes in the virus. (Dr. Jennifer Nuzzo, 5/13/20)

question: How can mayors help coordinate and supplement public health efforts at the state or county level?
original answer:
Just a few months ago, the idea that mayors would be fundamentally involved with medical testing would seem very odd to people, but a lot has happened since then. From a public health perspective, mayors may have the best view of the gaps. A mayor’s ability to recognize those gaps and then marshal the means—whether through moral authority, coordination, or direct investment—to plug them is an amazing transformation and very important for the control of a pandemic. (Dr. Josh Sharfstein, 5/13/20)

Cities can coordinate with other cities and towns in their county or look to coordinating bodies such as the California Conference of Local Health Officers (CCLHO) for help in aligning and collaborating county-wide public health efforts. Coordination efforts could involve directing testing resources to where they are needed most, supporting contact tracing, or creating task forces to address the needs of those living and working in assisted-living facilities or other high-risk living situations. Communication with county health departments is essential for cities to make strategic choices about when local action can effectively supplement county-level activities. (Dr. Josh Sharfstein, 4/29/20)

question: Can we expect federal support to help us balance local budgets?
original answer:
I don't think that the stimulus coming from Washington, however big, is going to solve this problem. It’s not going to be structured in a way that's most helpful to local governments. We'll probably see something, but not enough to fix the full problem. 

To the extent that stimulus helps states—where state bond banks can step in, for example, and make capital available to small businesses—it might enable you to take a small breath but won’t give you many more tools. You have to position yourselves in the hope that we finally have a major U.S. infrastructure program that creates jobs because that's the only place to create the economic multiplier that could really put the country into recovery. (Linda Bilmes, 5/13/20)

There are no easy or new answers to this question. Governments have been on a starvation diet in the U.S. for 30 years, maybe longer. Part of the challenge is the long game: people have to believe that they're getting value from government. If they ever needed evidence, looking around today at everything you are doing in cities to help people get through this crisis shows why government is first order essential to civilization as we know it. For an improvement in the climate, we must continue to demonstrate that government generates real value.

The best you can hope for from the federal government right now is that you may see some transitional relief. original answer:
These are unusual times, so the usual rules about micromanaging go out the window. You need to go through what's actually happening in the budget at a level of detail that is much different from business as usual, given the fiscal outlook. question: Any updates on potential treatments, like remdesivir or antibody-type therapies?
original answer:
Remdesivir is an antiviral treatment that had a positive result in one randomized controlled study, showing that it could cut the number of days in the hospital. The research is ongoing. You have to examine where in the process it’s given—it was being given quite late to very sick patients. There are other studies taking place using it earlier in the timeline to see if it could be more effective then. 

The studies on immunity are moving ahead, and there remains a fair amount of hope for the convalescent serum and other types of antibody products to provide some protection. It'll be about two months before we get results. Recent evidence has indicated that most people tend to make antibodies, which is good. We also know that there are antibodies that really do neutralize the virus. The most promising short-term treatment option could be antibody-type therapies, and perhaps in summer we'll get evidence that they provide some benefit. That could really help slow the spread, even if it's not available to everyone. Preventive antibody treatment could help safeguard first responders and healthcare workers or nursing home residents and staff. 

We’re still using social distancing to buy time for science to come to the rescue. There are many different scientists working on this challenge and so many different ways to approach it. We don't need everything to work. We just need a few things to work. We're in the difficult time before we get that breakthrough, and we're just trying to buy time for progress. (Dr. Josh Sharfstein, 5/13/20)

question: Can we go forward with outdoor summer programs for youth?
original answer:

You can do things at summer camps to reduce risk, but you can't eliminate it, so parents will have to make their own decisions. Being outside is definitely better than being inside. But the evidence tells us that kids can get infected and pass the infection on. You’re going to have a conversation with parents on one hand and camp operators on the other.

question: How should we prioritize testing as we begin expanding testing capacity in the community?
original answer:
The priority should be to test symptomatic people, but there are some populations where you probably want to test asymptomatic people as well, and nursing homes are a great place to start. I would recommend some level of surveillance testing for healthcare workers or others with high exposure risk. As tests become more available, you can expand testing capacity strategically, thinking through the frequency and sustainability of surveillance efforts in terms of test availability.

Having more tests does not necessarily mean you are doing a good job with your response. In some states, there are worrisome trends where the overall state test numbers look like they are improving, but then there are huge pockets of the state not being tested at all. This can be a problem in cities as well.

Being able to identify what parts of the community are not able to access testing is important. It may be particular neighborhoods or ethnic communities, or small businesses that are customer-facing, or those working in higher risk occupations, such as healthcare or first responders. Make these people priorities for whatever testing is available after you’ve covered testing for everyone with symptoms or contacts of known cases and everyone on the frontlines. question: What are the best ways to track and use data on the effects of the virus on racial and ethnic communities and subgroups?
original answer:
The more granular and specific we can get with the data, the more helpful it will be. Cities and hospitals can work with county or state health departments to get this information for the communities they serve. The CDC has made an effort to weight data based on the particular communities within a state, to account for the difference in distribution of people of different racial and ethnic groups across a larger geographic area. It’s even more informative to have the data at a zip code or neighborhood level, if possible.

We should also realize a lot of the data presented in the media is not adjusted for age. The white population is older, on average, than most populations of color. If we accounted for age differences, we would find that African Americans are actually dying at even higher rates than expected because they're younger than the white population. There are lots of other things that need to be taken into account, but more granular information is most helpful. (Dr. Lisa Cooper, 5/7/20)

question: What are some best practices for cross-pollinating expertise from different departments or teams to generate new ideas?
original answer:
Trying to generate new ideas with existing teams can be frustrating. This isn't because there’s anything wrong with your existing teams. In fact, they're the experts in what they're doing. But the problem is that they're “experts in the past,” and what you need are people to help you become experts in the future. You need what Michael Tushman and Charles O’Reilly would call an “ambidextrous organization.” You need parts of your organization continuing to do what they've done well in the past, supporting people in the community in ways they've always done. You also need the people who are going to explore the future.

When one mayor put an engineer in her homelessness working group, she got new solutions – fast. That is a perfect example of finding somebody who's maybe not an expert in community health but has expertise from other domains. The word “cross-pollination” is apt. The trick is to organize and lead these teams so that you get enough cross-pollination but avoid what they would call “cross-contamination”—for example, if, in the first minute, the engineer hears, "That's never going to work. You shouldn't do that. That's not allowed. Don't try that."

Your job is to push looking at the future, push execution in the present, and make sure people are connecting with each other, but not to mash them all into one team and say you're all innovators now. If you bring together good people who might have the capacity to be part of your innovation front, don't make it seem like they're better than other people. They're just available and they are there to look towards the future, while other people are working on the present, and they are going to have to communicate with each other. The last thing you want to do is create a schism. (Mitch Weiss, 5/5/20)

question: How are cities preparing for (hopefully, eventual) COVID-19 vaccination of all residents, especially in light of anti-vaccination sentiments in some corners?
original answer:
As we think about a COVID-19 vaccine, it is very important that you take on disinformation about vaccination. Begin to grease that path now, because once that vaccine is available, it will be too late. You don't want 40 percent of your citizens feeling vaccination is unsafe. (Juliette Kayyem, 5/20/20)

Many of the ideas and conspiracy theories propagated by anti-vaccine activists are rooted in distrust of authority. They need to be addressed head on with communications and social media campaigns, as well as efforts at the local level to work with wary communities about the necessity of vaccinations. Disinformation feeds a vacuum and mayor’s must utilize their professionals – doctors, trusted spokespeople – to counteract.  In addition, rules regarding access to schools or other “privileges” based on vaccination should be publicly enforced. (Juliette Kayyem, 5/5/20)

The success of a safe and effective vaccine will depend on its widespread use. To achieve herd immunity for measles, for example, at least 90-95% of the population needs to be vaccinated. The novel coronavirus appears to be somewhat less contagious than measles but achieving herd immunity would still require large majorities of the population to get vaccinated.

The CDC has published guidance on improving vaccine coverage. Cities can take steps to promote widespread vaccination, including requiring it for daycare and school entry and encouraging stronger healthcare practices, such as in-depth discussion with hesitant parents and establishing routine vaccination as the default for medical check-ups. (Dr. Josh Sharfstein, 5/5/20)

question: What can cities do to support teachers transitioning to an online learning format and parents transitioning to homeschooling for the first time?
original answer:
In the first instance, cities can facilitate the shift to online learning by working with schools, businesses, and nonprofits to ensure that every student has safe and regular access to the internet from home. Cities can also help provide forums and tools for teachers to share curriculum and lesson-planning ideas, and develop tools to assist parents and caregivers. 

Supporting remote learning is just one part of the education leadership that mayors can offer at this time, however. You can use your position to convene a children's cabinet or council to coordinate cross-boundary efforts to make sure students in your city are safe, healthy, well-fed, able to access mental and behavioral healthcare, and generally prepared to learn online or otherwise. 

Below are a few examples of what cities around the US are doing to help educators, caregivers, and students.

Wichita is providing online professional development for teachers every hour on the hour on how to provide blended learning. 

Orange County has developed a Parent Academy to train parents and caregivers to assist in providing high-quality education and assistance to students.  

Tacoma, Washington is hosting live weekly webinar series on topics including "Engaging Learners Online" and "Supporting Youth With Disabilities." 

Somerville, Massachusetts, has created a website with an Early Education Remote Learning Plan that includes links to learning resources. 

The By All Means initiative at Harvard's Graduate School of Education reports the following approaches from some of its partner cities:

In Louisville, KY, the district’s Teaching and Learning team developed an online portal for students and teachers to engage in remote learning. It also distributed instructional packets that students can complete without a digital device.  

In Oakland, CA, the school district has worked to promote equity by building a strong infrastructure to support online learning. Students have electronic devices and access to broadband connectivity. In addition, each school provides at-home learning plans to guide instruction.

In Chattanooga-Hamilton-County in TN, the school district is bolstering students’ learning opportunities by partnering with the local PBS station to offer educational programming. In addition, Chattanooga 2.0, a backbone organization supporting its "Children's Cabinet," launched a communications campaign to address the digital divide affecting many children and families in the community and has worked with businesses to purchase tech and secure free/low-cost internet access for all students.

Providence, RI, is tackling the digital divide through the state’s partnership with internet providers and cell phone carriers, which are offering unlimited data plans and free internet service for a period of time. (Lynne Sacks, 4/30/20)

question: What safeguards can we put in place to open the economy besides increased testing and contact tracing?
original answer:
In Singapore, the government had to clamp back down when there was a new outbreak that started in dormitories for migrant workers. The lesson there is to think about where you could have a big outbreak, and it may not be a place on your usual radar. It could be the jail, even if it’s a county run jail, or the plant where a lot of people work, or places with high-risk individuals like privately-run shelters for people experiencing homelessness or nursing homes. Pay close attention to those places, because cases can blow up quickly, seed a lot of infections, and lead to a lot of fear.

Keeping an eye on those places may not have been part of your day-to-day work prior to this epidemic, but you need be paying attention to them, thinking about what they may need, being in touch with their management, and talking to health officials about what can be done. (Dr. Josh Sharfstein, 4/29/20)

Given the political pressure, it’s inevitable that we are going to reopen in advance of what we might call the gold standard. So we need to think about this in a practical sense: What is the best we can do in a risky environment? Business and local leaders should begin thinking about re-engineering their operations. Every city is different, and every business operates differently. A lot of local ingenuity is needed to figure out how to continue to operate—or begin to re-operate—safely in the presence of COVID-19. (Dutch Leonard, 4/30/20)

question: What are some practical ideas for local government leaders to invite naysayers into the tent?
original answer:
Often during a crisis, there’s a rising level of conflict between people's sense of their interests over time. At the beginning, everybody gets it. Everybody's on the same side. The way to keep people together is to constantly remind people of the goals: the values at stake and the things that we're trying to work on together. When you remind people of what we all have in common, sometimes the conversation gets a little calmer. (Dutch Leonard, 4/30/20)

As the crisis extends and some of these divisions emerge, you can create new and different kinds of forums for that work to happen. Lincoln did this during the Civil War with some of the people he thought were his worst enemies within the Union—especially politicians and journalists. He sat them down, let them talk and listened to what they had to say. He called these experiences, like those he had with ordinary citizens, who lined up several days a week to see him in the White House, his “public opinion baths,” understanding that not only was he gaining a sense of who were the vocal, influential “doubting Thomases,” but also that he was giving these people a chance to say what they had to say. This allowed him to dial down some of those divisions and to remind people of what they were actually all trying to do. (Nancy Koehn, 4/29/20)

question: How can we address doubts, fear, and uncertainty among our team members—especially when we share the same feelings?
original answer:
What I have learned studying leaders is that it's very important to take deft, mindful opportunities to address people's fears. You want to display your humanity, and you want them to relate to you, but how can you do that without becoming so vulnerable that people lose confidence in you? That's the fine line you’re walking.

Think of Franklin Roosevelt's first inaugural address: “We have nothing to fear but fear itself.” You can address and acknowledge their fears, but you don't want to share too many of your own. Remember, your job as a leader is to help them “do harder, better things than they can get themselves to do on their own,” to help them navigate that inner uncertainty. (Nancy Koehn, 4/29/20)

You have to be brutally honest and still offer a rational basis for hope, with an emphasis on the latter. You also have to show empathy, but empathy doesn't mean that you dissolve in tears and say, “I don’t know what we're going to do. I don't know how we're going to make our way through this.” Ernest Shackleton never shamed anyone for weakness or their inability to do something. He ordered a round of warm milk for everybody. He also tried to model behavior. He was calm in the face of danger and that came across physically and viscerally to his followers. (Dutch Leonard, 4/30/20)

question: How do you assemble the right team for crisis response?
original answer:
Ernest Shackleton hired for attitude and trained for skill. He sought people who were comfortable in uncertainty and attitudinally ready for a very real, very serious challenge. Think about the attitude, the work ethic, and the resumé, but that's only part of a much broader set of criteria in hiring people for great uncertainty and high stakes situations. (Nancy Koehn, 4/29/20)

If you are recruiting for a dangerous and difficult mission, be blunt with people about how hard it will be. That way your applicants will be self-selected for toughness, or at least for thinking of themselves as tough. People who step forward are likely to be those who are comfortable in a very uncertain environment. Then you can look for ways to test for that: Who can actually demonstrate the necessary flexibility, the ability to work effectively across boundaries? (Dutch Leonard, 4/30/20)

See the take-aways document for Session #6, “Learning from History to Act Now and Prepare for the Future: Leading through a Multi-Stage Crisis,” for more information on Ernest Shackleton and leadership lessons from his polar expedition.

question: Are there benchmarks that we can use in virus reproduction rates, or number of days of decreasing infections that will help us know when to start to partially open up businesses again?
original answer:
You want the number of positives relative to the number of tests to be low. If it's too high, that suggests that you're probably only testing the sickest people. Before reopening, you want a reasonable estimate of how many people with infections are out there and could transmit their infection. So we need to test broadly, and to make an informed estimate, we need to understand what proportion of the population being tested is testing positive. (Dr. Jennifer Nuzzo, 4/29/20)

Ideally, we want to drive the reproductive rate (the average number of new cases resulting from a single case), but that will take some time to achieve. In the meantime, most people who are evaluating when to begin easing up of social distancing are looking at 14 days of declining cases as an important benchmark. Fourteen consecutive days of an incidence (the number of new cases that occur each day) would mean cases are declining so long as new cases aren’t being missed due to inadequate testing.

Some other things that mayors could consider monitoring as they begin to lift restrictions might include absenteeism data from major employers. This might function as an early sign of an emerging outbreak. Or you might collect data on whether people are wearing masks when and where they're supposed to be, or taking other precautions. (Dr. Josh Sharfstein, 4/29/20)

question: How can we help seniors isolated by social distancing feel socially connected?
original answer:
Caring for the mental health of elders in assisted living or nursing facilities, who are cut off from in-person visits from family as well as interaction with their peers, is an important part of responding to this crisis.

The city of Barcelona offers seniors an application called VinclesBCN to simplify communication by text messaging, photographs, or video for elderly smartphone and tablet users. It allows them to set up a personal network of family and friends as well as a group network of fellow seniors who live nearby or share common interests. It also helps connect them to local online activities.

The app now features a health channel, managed by medical professionals, to provide information on COVID-19 and answer users’ questions via text or voice message. (Dr. Jennifer Nuzzo, 4/29/20)

question: How can we get tests for all patients and staff at nursing homes?
original answer:
Mayors can talk to hospitals, labs, or health departments about setting aside testing for nursing homes, and then work to establish a team to go out and perform tests for patients and staff.

In Maryland, for example, there is a process where the health department identifies a nursing home outbreak, and then Johns Hopkins or another entity sends a team, with protective equipment, to test everyone and give advice on infection control. Mayors can play an important role in connecting parties to get the tests where they need to be. (Dr. Josh Sharfstein, 4/29/20)

You can use your position as mayor to advocate for the facilities in your community—especially as additional resources may be coming into the state, and nursing homes may experience challenges accessing them. You can step in and be their voice. (Dr. Jennifer Nuzzo, 4/29/20)

question: Would it be prudent to test all older adults living in senior housing sites for COVID-19?
original answer:
Ideally, we would not just be testing everybody with symptoms, but also doing contact tracing and testing all the people they may have exposed along the way. Ideally, we would be doing surveillance testing in all high-risk groups, for healthcare workers and perhaps seniors and those living in senior housing. However, I don't see us getting there soon.

In independent senior living communities specifically, when there is an outbreak, widespread testing is important to reduce further spread. For assisted living and nursing homes, regular testing of residents and staff is prudent, provided there are resources. Once outbreaks are detected, there should be aggressive testing to find everybody who may be infected. (Dr. Jennifer Nuzzo, 4/29/20)

question: Is the primary reason for COVID-19 spreading in nursing homes that workers float among various sites?
original answer:
There are many factors, and one is sharing staff, who may be bringing in an infection even if they do not have symptoms. That's why access to testing—especially once cases are found—is important, not just in that facility, but for all the facilities that may have shared staff over the past 14 days.

In an ideal world, we wouldn't be moving staff around between all these facilities and retroactively trying to identify where they potentially could have exposed lots of people. I'm not sure there's a solution other than dramatically expanding the workforce. It’s an issue that will come up when workers are not able to return to work and we start thinking about how to fill the gaps with volunteers. This is another reason why access to personal protective equipment and, we hope, routine screening is very important. (Dr. Jennifer Nuzzo, 4/29/20)

question: How can we hold nursing homes accountable when they are regulated by the state?
original answer:
It’s a challenging regulatory landscape, and accountability is important, but the goal for mayors should be to engage with these facilities and offer assistance, because these are enormous challenges, and they simply can't do it alone. The solutions to many of their problems are outside their facilities. Creating trusted partnerships and helping to solve problems should encourage transparency and accountability. Most nursing homes want to do right by their patients and just need additional tools to do so.

If we are creating a situation in which we are disincentivizing the reporting of cases by identifying individual facilities publicly, then I'm not sure how that helps us control COVID-19 or any other outbreak. (Dr. Jennifer Nuzzo, 4/29/20)

State regulatory authorities are stretched thin in these situations and need help. You can reach out to them with sympathy rather than reproach: “You’ve got your hands full trying to contain COVID-19 in nursing homes. You’ve put out guidance. question: How can we lead effectively in a shared governance structure, where detractors can undermine you?
original answer:
How you show up, your body language, and your general demeanor and energy make a difference. People are hungry for guidance, confidence, and seriousness of purpose, and they take their cues from all kinds of nonverbal behaviors. We need to get comfortable with a lot of uncertainty and chaos, with too little information and changing information, give others permission to not know what to do, and remind everyone that we are navigating point to point. We're navigating only to the next point, which is usually the point through which we think the waves are lowest and the winds the slowest.

question: What can cities do to ensure technology access for communities who do not have computers and internet access at home?
original answer:
To ensure internet reliability, cities can work directly with internet service providers. The Federal Communications Commission (FCC) issued the Keep Americans Connected Pledge, asking internet service providers to refrain from disconnecting consumers who fall behind in payments, waive late fees, and open up Wi-Fi hotspots across the country. A long list of companies has already signed on, including AT&T, CenturyLink, and Verizon. To supplement this service, cities such as Austin have deployed school buses equipped with Wi-Fi to neighborhoods and apartment complexes where there is the highest need for internet access.

question: How can we get more testing capacity, and how will it help me ease restrictions?

question: How should we respond to those arguing for lifting restrictions in order to achieve “herd immunity”?
original answer:
Herd immunity occurs when a large enough proportion of the population is immune to the virus to prevent it from finding enough suitable hosts to spread quickly. The primary way we achieve herd immunity to communicable diseases is through vaccination. In the absence of an effective vaccine, the only way to achieve herd immunity for a highly contagious disease is for a large majority of the population to become infected. Exposing the general population to the virus in a deliberate effort to achieve herd immunity would lead to a spike of new cases that could quickly overwhelm local health care systems, leading to widespread suffering and death.

If there are stakeholders in your area using the idea of herd immunity to argue for lifting restrictions, look to local public health officials, healthcare executives, or other credible experts who can help explain the implications of doing so. (Dr. Tom Frieden, 4/21/20)

question: How can frontline health care workers protect their families?
original answer: Infections among health care workers are not inevitable. Singapore has had over 1,000 infections and hardly any among health care workers. Those few infections that did occur appear to have happened in the community, not in health care. They did that not with high-tech interventions but by ensuring consistent practices and policies, not just with PPE but also through what is called the “hierarchy of controls.” Those are source control (e.g., patients not coming in unless very ill, and all patients wearing a mask), engineering control (e.g., partitions in triage areas), administrative controls (e.g., cohorting of health care workers to reduce transmission among them), and personal controls (PPE) so that you reduce the amount of virus and the exposures. Meticulous attention to detail is crucial. (Dr. Tom Frieden, 4/21/20)

question: How are towns planning for summer recreation programs that kids and families in underserved communities rely on?
original answer:
The virus is causing deep disruptions. It is important not just to address the immediate health concerns but also the many downstream effects. Summer programs are important to the mental and physical health of many communities, and it is important to find ways to reimagine them in light of the COVID-19 crisis. Cities don’t need to do this on their own—this is also a great opportunity to work with nonprofits and community organizations to reimagine and deliver these programs. For example, for soccer programs, coaches could prescribe drills and activities (with videos) that children complete on their own.

To address the needs of the community members (e.g., childcare), consider providing more direct support (e.g., stipends, rent freezes).

This is another example of “situational anticipation:” looking ahead to see what new problems are emerging. It creates an opportunity for convening a local group to brainstorm and creatively imagine new approaches that provide some of the intended benefits safely in the presence of COVID-19. (Dutch Leonard, 4/21/20)

What is also important to remember is that getting kids outdoors is also key to their resiliency. (Juliette Kayyem, 4/21/20)

question: How can we continue to protect the homeless—and other city residents and workers—in temporary shelters?
original answer:
Testing data from Boston showed that a third of unhoused people in the city’s shelters had coronavirus infections—in many cases without symptoms. This should worry other cities. People experiencing homelessness need facilities that allow for good sanitation, handwashing, and social distancing. Working with universities to utilize dormitory space or with the business community to create new shelter spaces or tents for hospital testing sites could be helpful. We need to be able to isolate and track people who test positive and care for them if they become acutely ill, which was tough before this pandemic started and is tougher now. (Dr. Howard Koh, 4/21/20)

Masks, frequent cleaning and keeping physical distance are all helpful, but it's going to be hard to control the spread as long as people are in big rooms and moving around. Look for ways to switch models so that you have people in more individual units. (Dr. Josh Sharfstein, 4/21/20)

Going forward, there’s a risk that if unstably housed people go back to the streets or into shelters with less health support and space for physical distancing, there could be a new outbreak. You have to weigh the need for people to go back to work against the possibility that, if you relax the extraordinary measures for vulnerable populations, you'll end up with an even bigger problem. (Dr. Tom Frieden, 4/21/20)

question: How can we address health disparities related to race, ethnicity, and wealth?
original answer:
We're seeing much higher infection and death rates among African Americans and, in some parts of the country, Latinos. That means we need to increase the sheltering and the shielding of the vulnerable populations, target them for testing and contact tracing, and work with communities to limit the spread.

We can work to build personal and community resilience by addressing some of the underlying conditions that are contributing to the greater vulnerability of communities of color, like lack of access to health care and higher rates of hypertension and diabetes. (Dr. Tom Frieden, 4/21/20)

These increased rates are a result of a constellation of factors, including greater representation among essential workers (who may not have had access to sufficient protective equipment), less opportunity for social distancing in crowded or unstable living arrangements, less ability to stay home because of income constraints, and greater levels of chronic illness.

Mayors can ask: If somebody does not have a doctor, how can they get testing and follow-up care, and have a safe place to isolate and quarantine? Public health authorities can set up call centers and special clinics to make sure everyone has access—not just to testing but also to services like food and medicine delivery.

Making sure that people are hearing reliable and relevant messages from people they trust in every community in your city is also important. Different rumors or myths get traction in different communities; these need to be tracked and countered effectively with the facts. We also need to invest in supporting low-wage essential employees, listen to their fears, take them seriously, and act to protect them. (Dr. Josh Sharfstein, 4/21/20)

question: What can we do to get cloth or paper masks to all residents?
original answer:
There is still a general shortage of masks, and medical-grade N95 masks are being reserved for health care workers. If you are able to source a large number of cloth or paper masks to offer your city’s residents, give priority to workers at essential businesses, those in crowded living situations (such as shelters), those taking public transportation, and others in high-risk communities. You can also help direct residents to the CDC’s guidelines for constructing homemade face coverings.

Mayors might also want to encourage virtual “sewing circles” in their communities to increase the supply of home-made masks for people who can’t make their own. This would give some people in the community a way to constructively contribute to fighting the virus, and also has the benefit of helping to reserve N95 and surgical masks for the people with greatest exposure – healthcare workers, public safety workers, and essential service providers. question: Can we do or prepare for contact tracing before there is widespread access to rapid testing?
original answer:
It is possible to get started on contact tracing before there's widespread testing. You could talk to your health department about setting up reporting of suspect cases and starting contact. If someone calls a call center and says, “I'm coughing, I have a fever and I can't smell,” then public health officials might be able to consider them as positive and start to trace their contacts. Even if you can't do that with everyone who calls and says they're coughing, you can get started with some of those presumptive cases. (Dr. Josh Sharfstein, 4/21/20)

Example: For cities and counties experiencing a surge in cases, contact tracing for every person has become difficult. Nassau County in New York has prioritized contact tracing for people who have had direct exposure to a lot of people, such as food handlers or residents in group homes. Cities and counties that may not have full contact tracing capacity can tell those who test positive to alert contacts on their own.

question: What can I do to build support and infrastructure for contact tracing?
original answer:
Start with local and state health departments and ask what they’re doing. If you do not have a public health department in your city, ask the county health department if staff is able to contact trace every case right now—and if they are, ask how many contacts they are able to find, and how isolation and quarantine are going. You might offer support, like food delivery to quarantined people, because it's not just about finding people who may have been exposed; it’s also about helping people quarantine. Stay in close contact with whatever public health entity is leading contact tracing—first to ensure that it's happening and second to be supportive. (Dr. Josh Sharfstein, 4/21/20)

Right now, state leaders are trying to prioritize how to spend the federal stimulus money. (Dr. Howard Koh, 4/21/20)

question: How can we scale up contact tracing?
original answer:
Contact tracing is a tried and true public health method. We do it for TB, sexually transmitted diseases, HIV, and for vaccine-preventable diseases such as measles. There's a whole set of skills that goes along with it. Contact tracing involves building trust with the patient and quickly warning the patient’s contacts. We absolutely have to protect privacy and confidentiality. When it's done well, public health earns, gains, and maintains patient trust and is able to get the most sensitive information reliably from people. Public health departments all over the country are overwhelmed and can't imagine working at ten or a hundred times the scale to make this successful, but people working together to build trust and understanding is what makes this work.

One of the best examples we can look to is Singapore, where, for a population of a few million, a thousand people are doing this full time. They do a video conference with every case. They track down 30 to 40 contacts per case and warn them. This is an enormous effort. There are emerging best practices. We can share some materials that we put together from around the country and around the world. This is a moving target. (Dr. Tom Frieden, 4/21/20)

Mayors can be very helpful in getting health departments to understand and embrace the scale up that's necessary. Some state and local governments, such as Massachusetts, New Haven, and San Francisco, are partnering with nonprofits including academic medical centers that have local and global public health knowledge.

In other places, they're using city or county employees such as school nurses to do contact tracing. Other areas are reaching out to universities and getting hundreds of students involved right away. Sometimes with these local departments there’s a small team for the usual contact tracing on STDs and HIV, and mayors can connect them to resources to help them figure out how to scale up. (Dr. Josh Sharfstein, 4/21/20)

There are underutilized human resources right now. A lot of students have been let out of school early and are eager to volunteer. Local public health departments have been under-resourced for a long time, so there are not nearly enough professionals to do contact tracing. (Dr. Howard Koh, 4/21/20)

Resource: The national contact tracing plan released by the Johns Hopkins Bloomberg School of Public Health and Association of State and Territorial Health Officials (ASTHO) recommends deploying over 100,000 contract tracers for a 12-month deployment, with Congress appropriating about $3.6 billion in emergency funding for state and local public health departments.

question: How long should social distancing last?
original answer:
We must look at data, not dates. Three preconditions must be met before a city can begin to gradually “open the faucet.” There are (1) falling case and death rates; (2) a health care system that can withstand a small outbreak without risk to workers and patients; and (3) a public health capacity to: test to identify people newly infected with coronavirus, isolate those who test positive, trace contacts who may have been exposed to people with active infections, and quarantine those individuals. I recommend creating a corps of trained contact tracers—possibly as many as one for every 1,000 residents—to locate potentially exposed individuals and support them through a fourteen-day quarantine. Watch for the CDC to publish guidelines in the near future.

Even with a strong public health response, the faucet has to be loosened slowly. The medically vulnerable should continue to stay home. Set priorities according to societal benefit and take measures to reduce risk, such as temperature checks and symptom checklists for workers, mandatory hand hygiene measures, and maintenance/use of sensor-operated doors and fixtures. Plan on tightening the faucet quickly if you see another spike in cases. (Dr. Tom Frieden, 4/14/2020)

question: How many contacts can a contact tracer reasonably keep up with?
original answer: The answer depends to some degree on the number of cases, the relative ease of finding contacts and on the resources available to contact tracers. In one city of China, they required nearly 1 contact tracer for every 1,000 people in the community. There's contact elicitation (finding out from the index case who their contacts are), then there's connecting with each of those contacts, who may be more or less easy to find. Sometimes an individual patient can infect a lot of people. In those super-spreading events, we really need to go wide, and work intensively to find all of the cases and contacts. There may be electronic tools that will make the process more efficient, but that's at least a month or two away and not yet proven. These tools are NOT the same as what is being discussed as finding contacts by using cell phone proximity, nor are they the same as tracking the location of contacts and cases to see if they are adhering to quarantine and isolation. (Dr. Tom Frieden, 4/14/20)

question: I am worried about the essential staff who have carried the burden of keeping the city government and other institutions operating, like medical workers. How do we help them?
original answer:
During crises, municipal workers still on the job must balance the demands of a significantly expanded workload with heightened obligations and stress in their personal lives. As mayor, it is important that you provide them the support that they need – most importantly for their own wellbeing but also so they can perform the city’s work as best they can during such a difficult time. To start, you should ensure that they are working in as safe an environment as possible. For COVID-19, this includes providing them with sanitizers, masks and other forms of protection (e.g., gloves or, depending on the setting, plastic/glass barriers). They should also have access to health services to address any physical or mental health issues they may experience.

It is important to be responsive to their needs on an ongoing basis. To ensure municipal employees’ work is as seamless and safe as possible over the full course of the pandemic, you should establish feedback systems that allow you to engage directly and regularly with staff about these issues. One way of doing so is to take time in daily meetings with department heads and senior advisors to surface and address their employees’ concerns. These meetings may largely focus on the city’s crisis response to the pandemic – but by also prioritizing your workers’ wellbeing, you will demonstrate the importance the issue should have across all of city government.

You can show your support in a number of other ways as well. Consider making time to speak with the workers in your city directly (e.g., through live web- or teleconferences), sending personal letters of support, or making public displays of gratitude. This is also a great opportunity to get your citizens involved. For example, citizens could send care packages or messages of thanks. Local celebrities could record a video of support; students and children can write messages with chalk.

Finally, burnout is a very real possibility during crises – especially among senior staff, who often end up working long hours under considerable stress and pressure. Because the response to the pandemic will be drawn out over several months, it is important to make sure they get time off to rest and recharge at appropriate intervals. (Juliette Kayyem, 4/11/20)

question: How will we know when it is safe to re-open businesses safely and responsibly?
original answer:
It is almost certainly too early to open non-essential businesses in most parts of the country. The number of new cases per day in the US is still growing at an exponential rate. While the spread of the virus may be hitting its projected peak in a handful of regions, it likely has not yet reached this mark in most others. Until entire regions see a meaningful and persistent reduction in the number of new cases per day, it is not recommended that communities in these regions re-open non-essential businesses.

When it is time to re-open non-essential businesses, we must do so gradually and carefully. By re-opening businesses in waves and at limited capacity, we will be better positioned to contain any future spread of the virus and implement the techniques that we know work: testing, isolation, and contact tracing. Juliette Kayyem and Joseph Allen wrote in USA Today, “If we don’t use these next two months wisely…then the weeks of social distancing we have already done, at great expense to our economy, will be for naught. In other words, we’ll be back right at the beginning as soon as we let up.” (Juliette Kayyem, 4/11/20)

See Juliette Kayyem’s framework, The Five Stages of Crisis Management; Coronavirus (COVID-19) in the US for information on the “Adaptive Recovery” stage of the COVID-19 crisis.

At present, consensus among government leaders and health officials is that the best way to defeat the virus is to order nonessential businesses to close and residents to confine themselves at home and maintain social distancing practices. Relaxing these restrictions could risk a new surge in infections and deaths, overwhelming an already stressed healthcare system, creating additional uncertainty among consumers, and ultimately resulting in a deeper, longer-lasting negative impact on economic growth.

There is no consensus on the best way to resume economic activity or social gatherings yet. In countries like South Korea and China, non-essential businesses reopened only after the number of new cases per day was brought to zero. Some experts have recently stated that it could be safe to gradually re-open businesses when a state reports a sustained reduction in cases for at least 14 days (i.e., one incubation period); and local hospitals are safely able to treat all patients requiring hospitalization without resorting to crisis standards of care; and the capacity exists in the state to test all people with COVID-19 symptoms, along with state capacity to conduct active monitoring of all confirmed cases and their contacts. But non-essential businesses should not just “reopen” – they should redesign their processes and procedures to maintain safety in a coronavirus-present reality. Helping them think through what they can do to reopen safely should be an emerging focus of problem-solving work locally. (Dutch Leonard, 4/1/20)

question: How have cities helped low income people take action to get stimulus direct deposit and checks to help stabilize families?
original answer:
If residents have filed taxes in 2018 or 2019, or they did not file taxes but receive Social Security payments, the IRS will automatically send stimulus payments to individuals and families. Individuals that have previously paid or received tax reimbursements with direct deposits should receive their money by mid-April. If the IRS doesn't have your bank information, it will send a paper check to your last known address. Those checks will be sent out starting at the end of April through early September.

However, the Tax Policy Center at the Brookings Institution estimates that there are as many as 10 million low-income, childless adults in the United States who are eligible for the federal government's stimulus payment program, but are at risk of missing out on the money because they have not filed taxes and do not participate in Social Security programs.

If you don't file taxes or get Social Security, the IRS and TurboTax have created an online portal to submit information on their direct-deposit details or mailing address and choose how they want to receive their stimulus check. Cities can utilize the infrastructure they have as part of their free tax prep programs or set up a virtual service that does outreach to low-income residents to ensure they have either filed in the past two years or registered with the IRS to receive payments.

Cities can also build people awareness about the stimulus payment scamming. The IRS has issued guidelines to help individuals discern what engagement is real. (Juliette Kayyem, 4/11/20)

question: How will cities and towns acquire needed funds?

question: Is there official guidance on the efficacy of DIY face masks, and can these be donated for use in healthcare settings?
original answer:

If used properly and in conjunction with social distancing techniques, cloth masks can help slow the spread of the virus in the general population. question: What are the disparities in testing for marginalized communities and how can we address them?
original answer:
We’ve largely built testing off our health care system, with all the inequities built into it. That's one of the reasons we're suggesting a call center that’s available to everyone. Even though this virus started in the United States with people returning from cruises or international travel, the populations at greatest risk are low-income, minority communities with high rates of chronic illness and insecure housing and food. The initial attention to people who got coronavirus on cruises and international trips has distracted us from the urgency of providing not just testing but also follow-up services—food, housing, and other supports—for vulnerable populations. It’s the right thing to do as a matter of justice, but it’s also absolutely critical for control of the disease. (Dr. Josh Sharfstein, 4/6/20)

Supplemental resources (4/7/20):

NPR reported on a recent study that shows doctors may be less likely to refer African Americans for testing when they show up for care with signs of infection. The bio-tech data firm Rubix Life Sciences, based in Boston, reviewed recent billing information in several states, and found that an African American with symptoms like cough and fever was less likely to be given one of the scarce coronavirus tests. However, at present, demographic data on coronavirus testing has not been widely disclosed and published. Recently, U.S. Senator Elizabeth Warren and Representative Ayanna Pressley have called on the federal Department of Health and Human Services to track racial data and address disparities in the national response to the coronavirus outbreak. In the meantime, cities like Milwaukee and Chicago are tracking COVID-19 data by race, which allows city officials to see and respond to disparities.

question: How do we balance the more positive, uplifting messages with more serious messaging around preparation and urgency?
original answer:
It’s true that we are sending inconsistent messages: “Take this seriously but be calm. Stay apart but come together.” It's hard to balance, but the basic truisms of communication do apply: be clear, concise, credible and consistent.

It cannot all fall to you. Bring people to the table and make sure they have your back. Try to communicate to different populations using the people in city government who are part of that group. If you have a 23-year-old hipster who knows some social media platform that you and I have never heard of, have him use it. Or record your mother or your father talking about you in a funny way and send it out as a robocall. Use whatever messengers you can find in creative ways to echo the message you're trying to get across.

You can only be yourself. But there is good data out there that shows social distancing is working. Constantly repeat that. Consider using more active language. I now call it mobilizing at home, and it empowers people to realize they're part of this solution—part of the team rather than isolated. (Juliette Kayyem, 4/6/20)

City Councilors and other city officials can use their networks to make doctors and other experts available for call-in sessions. These can, reach a lot of people with helpful messages and answer questions. (Dr. Josh Sharfstein, 4/6/20)

Be cautious about dividing reassuring and cautionary messaging between different spokespeople. If you do that, then it looks like there's a conflict between the messengers and the message gets muddy. Try instead to put those two messages together and explain that the reason there is (some, modest) good news to report is that people are complying. Otherwise people pick the message or the messenger they like best, and that's not going to generate a good outcome. (Dutch Leonard, 4/6/20)

question: How can we help people experiencing addiction and substance abuse issues?

question: Do you have advice for municipalities about the potential budgetary impact?
original answer:
Businesses can already see that if we run debt repayment and bankruptcy as we do in ordinary times, a vast number of organizations around the world will be bankrupted. If we default to those rules, it would needlessly destroy the ability of many of these businesses to recover. Private equity and other investors or creditors are showing flexibility in working with private-sector borrowers in order to keep the whole ecosystem going. They are going to have to do the same thing in municipal finance. While the usual rules may apply on a good day, this is not a good day. The CARES Act is designed in part to provide a flow of funds to consumers so that businesses still have revenue. We haven't done that yet with the municipal side, but this is a challenge that’s coming, and there will have to be a policy approach that resembles the flexibility we’re seeing on the business side. (Dutch Leonard, 4/6/20)

question: What questions do we need to ask or answer right now in order to start thinking about a plan for a swift and equitable recovery?
original answer:
It’s important to start thinking about recovery because it signals to people there will be another side to this. We can't tell you when that's going to be, but there's going to be a time beyond and we can start thinking about it now.

Lots of businesses are having challenges getting the capital that they need to keep going right now – so that should be an immediate priority. But just the process of convening a group of business leaders to start thinking about the aftermath is a sign of hope. In the aftermath of World War II, we knew millions of people would be flooding back into the labor market. Business leaders were brought together around the country to try to figure out how to do that locally. It’s probably too early to try to put policies in place, and you have to be careful not to signal that we're on the downside of the slope, but it's not too early to contemplate and start working together on the longer-term issues. (Dutch Leonard, 4/6/20)

This won’t be a case of, “Now we're ready, flip the switch.” It's going to be gradual. An important question to bring up with businesses is, what could that look like? How do you operate at a level of one or two out of ten? In Singapore, for example, they had restaurants open but with tape blocking every other chair. The more you can think about and plan those gradations, the more you may feel comfortable saying, “Okay, everyone, let's go to phase one." (Dr. Josh Sharfstein, 4/6/20)

What just happened may have felt like the flip of an on-off switch, but we need to think about recovery as a dimmer. It’s going to go up slowly, then it might have to come back down in response to a local outbreak. Business leaders also have to think about how to move from six or seven out of ten back down to two? There is tremendous work going on in this regard and we are learning from other countries, often the risks of what happens if they open too soon. (Juliette Kayyem, 4/6/20)

If you're investing in public health solutions, building that call center or the capacity to isolate and trace and quarantine, then you're going to be able to stay higher on that dimmer switch longer. It’s an investment in being able to turn on more things faster. In Singapore, they have hundreds of people to jump on infections when they happen and that gives them confidence to be able to open businesses. (Dr. Josh Sharfstein, 4/6/20)

question: My city doesn't have its own dedicated health officer because the health department is run by the county. What actions should we be taking to make sure all bases are covered?
original answer: The county health department should be actively engaged in your city’s response and helping to brief citizens. If the health department is not, you should raise targeted questions about important issues like the county’s plan for testing, contract tracing, isolation, and quarantine. However, I would encourage striking a constructive tone. It's not just, ''Are you doing these things?'' but, ''How can I help you do these things?'' The amount of contact-tracing and support for isolation that will be necessary far exceeds what any jurisdiction or local public health department can do. One of the most important roles for mayors is to mobilize the business community (especially hotels) and universities. Offer and solicit help from all quarters. (Dr. Josh Sharfstein, 4/4/20)
